papers.title: Constraint-Preserving Quantum Circuit Compilation for Graph Independent Sets via Persistent Occupancy Encoding
papers.abstract: Constraint-preserving mixers for graph independent sets repeatedly evaluate overlapping neighborhood conditions, increasing CX costs across ordered quantum optimization circuits. We propose a structure-aware compiler that reuses these conditions through persistent occupancy encoding. Exploiting mutual exclusion within true-twin classes, our reversible encoding stores class occupancy on the original data register across mixer operations and cost layers. Local mixers are synthesized using target compensation, blockwise parity queries, and coherent restoration; nonuniform cost phases are preserved by an exact coefficient transformation. We prove that the compiled circuit reproduces the original program's unitary action on the feasible subspace for any prescribed operation order and independent layer parameters, and establish exact separability of source-level caching costs under a fixed synthesis recipe. Across 134 evaluation programs and 72 independent confirmation programs, total CX counts fall by 22.61% and 19.87%, respectively, relative to the best of six reference implementations selected per program. Against a matched no-cache implementation, persistent encoding yields additional reductions of 4.10% and 9.13%.

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Risk Portfolio Optimization via Exponential Tilting
papers.abstract: Financial portfolio optimization is often framed through mean-variance objectives, yet real profit-and-loss (P&L) scenario distributions are typically discrete and non-Gaussian. To explore realistic P&L distributions, we propose an objective function based on exponential tilting and certainty equivalent under constant absolute risk aversion. We then derive a second-order approximation, recovering a quadratic optimization problem solvable through mixed integer quadratic programming (MIQP) and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). Constraints in the QUBO formulation are incorporated via Lagrangian relaxation and slack variable approaches, enabling a direct comparison between classical constrained MIQP and quantum-inspired methods. In order to study how exponential tilting affects mean, standard deviation, and tail-risk measures such as Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk, we design an experimental protocol based on scanning a grid of tilt parameters and solving the associated optimization problems. The results on a realistic trading portfolio show how the tilts can be tuned to optimize different risk-return profiles while remaining competitive with those found using other state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, performance analysis suggests that, even using classical solvers, the QUBO formulation with Lagrangian relaxation scales better than the MIQP approach, providing the best constraint encoding strategy.

papers.title: Q-TRACE: Physics-based zero-day attack detection for decoy-state quantum key distribution
authors: Sumit Tapas Chongder (Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur
papers.abstract: Practical quantum key distribution (QKD) is secure only while its devices match the assumptions of the security proof, and implementation attacks exploit mismatches while keeping the quantum bit error rate (QBER) low. We formulate attack detection in decoy-state BB84 as a sequential test against the honest-device manifold, the set of receiver statistics an attack-free link can produce under arbitrary channel loss. The resulting monitor, Q-TRACE (Quantum Telemetry Residuals Against Calibrated Expectations), calibrates a physical model of each link on commissioning data, profiles out the transmittance, and combines omnibus residual, physics score and setting-allocation tests with drift-robust references; no attack data are used. The formulation also yields a detectability exponent D* that lower-bounds the delay of any telemetry monitor and vanishes for a Trojan-horse probe with filtered back-reflection. On a count-level twin with model mismatch, over five held-out seeds and at a per-window false-alarm rate of 10^-3, Q-TRACE detects 63.6% of links under known attacks, 28.0% under unseen attack families and 65.3% under composite attacks, versus at most 51.2%, 6.7% and 42.3% for industry monitors, unsupervised and quantum-kernel detectors and a supervised classifier. Its delay attains the bound for strongly detectable attacks. On 33 parallel BB84 links of the IBM Heron processor ibm_marrakesh with physically executed entangling and amplitude-damping eavesdroppers, the measured information-disturbance relations agree with theory; a commissioning reference acquired under different operating conditions triggers alarms in every monitor tested, while a condition-matched reference detects a probe with 0.3% ideal QBER increase on 14 of 14 link-epochs with no false alarm on 66 honest ones.

papers.title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.

papers.title: Feed-Forward Dimension Control for High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution over Time-Varying Airborne Free-Space Links
papers.abstract: High-dimensional quantum key distribution tolerates more noise than qubit-based protocols, but the dimension that maximizes the secret key depends on turbulence, background light, device imperfections, and block size, all of which change during an airborne or satellite pass. Finite-size security analyses of high-dimensional protocols fix the dimension in advance, and the dimension-adaptive schemes reported so far have been analyzed only asymptotically. Here, a controller sets the dimension, acceptance thresholds, and key length of each block using only public data from earlier blocks. Each block is therefore a standard fixed-length protocol, and composable finite-key security against coherent attacks follows from sequential composition; an inaccurate channel model reduces the key rate but does not weaken security. The controller estimates turbulence from observed error rates, maximizes the expected key under forecast uncertainty, and recalibrates its model online. We evaluate it on a simulated entanglement-based orbital-angular-momentum link between an aircraft and a ground station, using Kolmogorov phase screens and the Hufnagel--Valley turbulence profile. Accounting for forecast uncertainty increases the key by 31\%--47\% relative to a naive planner. Over night, dawn, daytime, and model-mismatch scenarios, the recalibrated controller retains at least 98.8\% of the key obtained with the best fixed dimension for each scenario, while every fixed dimension drops to 73.5\% or less in at least one scenario. Running the link's measurement statistics on a superconducting quantum processor shows device errors close to a constant offset; with these errors included, the best daytime dimension changes from eight to four, and the controller adjusts accordingly.

papers.title: Estimating a Transition Point from Gibbs and Ground States
papers.abstract: We study how observed many-body system size affects the number of state copies needed to estimate a zero-temperature first-order transition point. The unknown Hamiltonian has bounded, translation-invariant on-site and nearest-neighbour interactions on a 3D cubic lattice with local dimension three. The field coupling is known, and all models share a known boundary field penalizing one local level. The limiting order parameter is uniformly separated across the transition. Each query returns an independently prepared Gibbs or ground state at an adaptive field and system size. For error $\epsilon$ and fixed confidence, we prove an exponential separation between two size caps at the same temperature. There are absolute constants $0<c_0<C$ and $c_1>0$ such that, at inverse temperature $\beta=c_1/\epsilon$, restricting side lengths to $L\le c_0/\epsilon$ requires $\exp(\Omega(1/\epsilon))$ copies in worst-case expectation, even with collective measurements. Allowing $L\le C/\epsilon$ permits $O(\log^2(1/\epsilon))$ copies and $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ total spins, using local measurements and polynomial classical postprocessing. The minimax expected total spin count is $\Theta(\epsilon^{-3})$ uniformly for $\beta\ge c_1/\epsilon$. At fixed positive temperature it is $\Theta_\beta(\epsilon^{-2})$, attained from one- and eight-site Gibbs states followed by exponential classical computation. For ground-state copies it is $\Theta(\epsilon^{-3})$. The lower bound uses a three-state ferromagnet whose boundary suppresses the sector carrying transition information. A spanning-forest argument and edge-boundary counting control its Gibbs weight uniformly over fields and allowed sizes, and a trace-distance hybrid argument handles adaptive learners with quantum memory. The upper bound combines finite-volume free-energy estimates, concavity and local order-parameter measurements.

papers.title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
papers.abstract: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot. On Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, LoRA reaches 83.9%, tying a 4-shot prompt (83.1%), but generalizes worse to unseen style (48.5% vs. 65.5%) and cuts QuantumKatas from 23.8% to 8.9%; on Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, LoRA beats the prompt overall (92.0% vs. 82.8%) and on unseen style (78.5% vs. 65.0%), and on the 1.5B model as well, so whether fine-tuning pays off depends on the base model, while the Qiskit regression appears in all three. Mixing two replay formats is the best mitigation trade-off (84.4% translation, Katas 21.5%). On 48 parametric functions that must become kernels with arguments -- where executing the input cannot yield a parametric kernel -- models reach up to 83%; on 27 real QED-C kernels, every model scores 0%. Language models can do source-level translation of simple parametric code, but not yet of real programs.

papers.title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
papers.abstract: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.

papers.title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
papers.abstract: In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

papers.title: Two messages suffice for quantum interactive proof systems
papers.abstract: Quantum interactive proof systems can be parallelized to three messages, as shown by Kitaev and Watrous (STOC 2000), perhaps their most striking distinction from classical counterparts. In this work, we establish that any quantum interactive proof system can further be parallelized to two messages, with the verifier sending halves of EPR pairs (``quantum public coins'') and, after the prover's response, using only stoquastic verification. Technically, we strengthen ${\sf QIP}(3) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}$ of Jain, Ji, Upadhyay, and Watrous (JACM, 2011) and fully characterize two-message quantum interactive proof systems by proving \[ {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf StoqAM} = {\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM} = {\sf QIP}(2) = {\sf QIP} = {\sf PSPACE}. \] Our main technical contributions show that Close Image to Uniform (CIUniform), which is naturally in the stoquastic version of ${\rm qq}\text{-}{\sf QAM}$, is $\sf PSPACE$-hard via transforming the sum-check protocol of Shamir (JACM, 1992) and Shen (JACM, 1992) into a CIUniform instance consisting of an efficient sampler whose image distribution is exactly uniform for some input distribution when the underlying quantified Boolean formula is true.

papers.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
papers.abstract: L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.

papers.title: Benchmarking Quantum Machine Learning for Power-System Attack Detection: Evaluation Choices Can Decide the Outcome
papers.abstract: Quantum machine learning is proposed to detect grid cyberattacks, but no study we could read tests quantum and classical detectors under white-box, transfer, and black-box attacks and random label flips in one protocol. We compare two quantum and six classical detectors on public grid-attack data under equal tuning budgets. Our main finding: evaluation choices can decide the outcome. On these data, seven choices each changed a reported result with model families fixed. Row-level splits inflate our best score by 0.31 macro-averaged F1 over held-out files, where matched-dimensionality classical and quantum models barely clear chance. Under its own white-box attack the quantum kernel's score falls from 0.56 to 0.01 (chance 0.50), while a transferred attack in the same run leaves 0.52. Trees admit no gradient-based white-box attack, so their attacked scores are upper bounds. These attack results use eight-dimension detectors under row-level splits. On gas-pipeline and simulated-grid data, neither quantum detector is more accurate or consistently more robust; three of the seven choices reproduce fully on gas data with one pressure feature log-scaled (two within noise), and none of the four checked on the grids does. Benchmarks should hold out whole files and give every model its own attack where possible. We release code and checklist.

papers.title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
papers.abstract: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $\beta$ to precision $\delta$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\beta,\log(1/\delta))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $\delta$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/\delta))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\beta,\log(1/\delta))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $\delta$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $\beta$ and linear in $1/\delta$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(\beta)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

papers.title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
papers.abstract: The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.

papers.title: Fermion-to-Fermion Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
papers.abstract: Simulating fermionic systems on qubit-based quantum computers often demands significant computational resources due to the requirement to map fermions to qubits. Thus, designing a fault-tolerant quantum computer that operates directly with fermions offers an effective solution to this challenge. Here, we introduce a protocol for fault-tolerant fermionic quantum computation utilizing fermion-to-fermion low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Our architecture employs a fermionic LDPC memory, which transfers its state to fermionic color code processors, where logical operations are subsequently performed. We use odd-weight logical Majorana operators to encode fermionic information in the LDPC memory and provide an algorithm for identifying these operators. Explicit code examples exhibit logical failure rates substantially below the physical error rate. We further develop two fermionic lattice surgery protocols to enable state transfer between the memory and processors. Finally, we demonstrate effective error suppression in a simulation of fermionic dynamics using the proposed protocol.

papers.title: Sublinear Time Quantum Algorithm for Attention Approximation
papers.abstract: Given the query, key and value matrices $Q, K, V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, the attention module is defined as $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)=D^{-1}AV$ where $A=\exp(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})$ with $\exp(\cdot)$ applied entrywise, $D=\mathrm{diag}(A\mathbf{1}_n)$. The attention module is the backbone of modern transformers and large language models, but explicitly forming the softmax matrix $D^{-1}A$ incurs $\Omega(n^2)$ time, motivating numerous approximation schemes that reduce runtime to $\widetilde O(nd)$ via sparsity or low-rank factorization. We propose a quantum data structure that approximates any row of $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)$ using only row queries to $Q, K, V$. Our algorithm preprocesses these matrices in $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1} n^{0.5} (s_\lambda^{3} + s_\lambda^{2} d + d) + \epsilon^{-2} s_\lambda d)$ time, where $\epsilon$ is the target accuracy and $s_\lambda$ is the $\lambda$-statistical dimension of the exponential kernel defined by $Q$ and $K$. Each row query can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(s_\lambda^2 + s_\lambda d)$ time. If every row sum of $A$ exceeds $\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n$, then with probability $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ the answers have Frobenius-norm error $O(\beta\|D^{-1}\|(\epsilon\|A\|_F+\lambda\sqrt n)\|V\|_F)$. Here $\beta=(1-(\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n)\|D^{-1}\|)^{-1}\geq 1$ is close to $1$ when every row sum is much larger than $\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n$. To our knowledge, this is the first quantum data structure that approximates rows of the attention matrix in sublinear time with respect to $n$. Our approach relies on a quantum Nystr\"om approximation of the exponential kernel, quantum multivariate mean estimation for computing $D$, and quantum sampling of the rows of $V$ by their squared norms, with a median over independent samples, for the multiplication with $V$.

papers.title: Four Ways to Stream: Exponential Separations from Random Order and Quantum Memory
papers.abstract: A streaming algorithm can keep classical or quantum memory, and its input arrives in adversarial or random order. Each resource alone is known to beat the basic model exponentially, but it was not known whether random order can help a quantum algorithm. We compare the four models by exponential space separations: every pair is separated on some problem and tied on another, and the two models with one resource each beat each other on different problems, one direction for random inputs, by concurrent work of Bouland, Ding, and Jain. The new phenomenon is that quantum memory and random order together can be exponentially stronger than each alone. We show this on a streaming version of Hidden Matching in which the bits of $x\in\{0,1\}^N$ arrive many times and $m\le\sqrt{N}$ matching requests must be answered on arrival. In random order a quantum algorithm uses $O(\log N\log m)$ space, while classical algorithms need $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$, and quantum algorithms need $\Omega(m)$ when all data comes before the requests. Two properties explain this. Consumability: answering a request destroys the quantum state. Replenishment: the state can be rebuilt from bits that keep arriving, which random order supplies and a data-first order does not. We prove that one quantum message answering $m$ Hidden Matching requests needs $\Omega(m)$ qubits, a conjecture of Gilboa, Jain, and McClean, for $m\le N^{1/2-\delta}$. The rest comes from Noisy Gap Cycle, a problem of Assadi and Sundaresan: tell whether a graph is a union of cycles of length $k$ or $2k$. With long cycles it needs linear space in all four models: we extend their random-order lower bound to quantum algorithms and obtain the first quantum random-order lower bounds for natural graph problems. With short cycles, $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ classical bits suffice in random order, but adversarial order requires polynomial quantum space.

papers.title: An Alphabet-Size Bound for the Information Bottleneck Function
papers.abstract: The information bottleneck function gives a measure of optimal preservation of correlation between some random variable $X$ and some side information $Y$ while compressing $X$ into a new random variable $W$ with bounded remaining correlation to $X$. As such, the information bottleneck has found many natural applications in machine learning, coding and video compression. The main objective in order to calculate the information bottleneck is to find the optimal representation on $W$. This could in principle be arbitrarily complicated, but fortunately it is known that the cardinality of $W$ can be restricted as $|{\cal W}|\leq|{\cal X}|+1$ which makes the calculation possible for finite $|{\cal X}|$. Now, for many practical applications, e.g. in machine learning, $X$ represents a potentially very large data space, while $Y$ is from a comparably small set of labels. This raises the question whether the known cardinality bound can be improved in such situations. We show that the information bottleneck function can always be approximated up to an error $\delta(\epsilon,|{\cal Y}|)$ with a cardinality $|{\cal W}| \leq f(\epsilon,|{\cal Y}|)$, for explicitly given functions $\delta$ and $f$ of an approximation parameter $\epsilon>0$ and the cardinality of ${\cal Y}$. Finally, we generalize the known cardinality bounds to the case were some of the random variables represent quantum information.

papers.title: Coherent Recovery of Nested Codes over the Quantum Erasure Channel Using Erasure Decoding and Quantization
papers.abstract: Motivated by quantum capacity results, we revisit nested binary linear codes for the quantum erasure channel through a packing-covering viewpoint: the outer code supports erasure reconstruction, while the inner code performs erasure quantization. We turn this perspective into two explicit decoder architectures. Architecture I requires no stabilizer-syndrome measurements and combines a classical peeling decoder and erasure quantizer with corresponding coherent quantum reconstruction and cleanup operations that disentangle the logical state from inaccessible erasure-environment branches. Architecture II goes one step further and implements erasure belief propagation directly through reversible ternary quantum gates, providing quantum state healing that reconstructs erased symbols while leaving unerased code states unperturbed. We establish sufficient conditions for exact recovery of arbitrary logical states, and illustrate both architectures using the Steane code, including explicit scheduling procedures and coherent quantum circuits.

papers.title: Mitigating large circuits with a learned small-circuit mitigator
papers.abstract: Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90\% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.

papers.title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
papers.abstract: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

papers.title: Increasing Quantum LDPC Code Distance through Explicit Extensions
papers.abstract: We give an explicit construction of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes without searching for candidates at each size. A fixed pair partition (PP) and fixed integer parameters determine the parity-check matrices at a specified size. Using affine permutation matrices (APMs), we construct a $[[3072,772,32]]$ code with column weight 3 and check weight 8 in each of the X and Z parity-check matrices. A construction based on circulant permutation matrices (CPMs) gives $[[1270,260,\ge34]]$, with column weight 4 and check weight 10. We prove that the construction yields commuting checks and verify the resulting distances using exhaustive search and logical operators. For the main construction, we conjecture the existence of a finite structural distance upper bound and distance improvement toward that bound as the size increases.

papers.title: Quantum Subentropy: Subadditivity and Sharp Bounds on Discrimination Error
papers.abstract: Subentropy gives a tight spectral lower bound on the accessible information of ensembles of pure states. We prove its subadditivity for arbitrary bipartite states in finite dimensions and derive a sharp relation between conditional subentropy and the minimum discrimination error. This relation strengthens a conjectured comparison with conditional min-entropy. Its inverse gives the strongest universal lower bound on the error determined only by conditional subentropy and the number of labels. Both main results follow from a comparison of conditional subentropy with the average subentropy of measurement posteriors, valid for mixed signal states and every finite measurement. We characterize all equality cases in these two results and bound posterior deviations near equality. We also determine the optimal Lipschitz constant in trace distance for conditional subentropy on classical-quantum states, including the exact constant when the quantum marginal is fixed. A determinant inequality strengthens subadditivity and proves strong subadditivity for classical distributions, while an exact counterexample shows that strong subadditivity fails for quantum states. Lean 4 proofs of all theoretical results are available at https://pratikpatil.io/lean/subentropy/

papers.title: Quantum Cyclic XYZ Stabilizer Codes
papers.abstract: XYZ codes generalize the Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) framework by adding $\sym{Y}$-type stabilizers to the usual $\sym{X}$- and $\sym{Z}$-type ones. We study XYZ codes whose three classical component codes are binary cyclic codes of odd length~$n$. Assigning disjoint sets of irreducible factors of $x^n-1$ to the three Pauli types fixes the number of encoded logical qubits and ensures that the row spaces of the three parity-check matrices intersect pairwise trivially. Then, a coprimality condition between the factors assigned to each type and the reciprocals of those assigned to the others guarantees the required orthogonality. Cyclotomic cosets give a complete and explicit description of the resulting family. We show that, for odd~$n$, a cyclic stabilizer code admits an XYZ representation with cyclic component codes iff its stabilizer generators are invariant, up to a phase, under the qubit permutation $i\mapsto 2i\bmod n$. By fixing the length and the dimension of the code, the proposed cyclic XYZ codes attain the best known minimum distance of stabilizer codes, exceed the minimum distance of the underlying CSS codes, and even exceed the linear-programming upper bounds for general CSS codes.

papers.title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
papers.abstract: Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

papers.title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels
papers.abstract: Antidegradable quantum channels have zero capacity for reliable quantum communication. However, they can nevertheless transmit quantum information with nontrivial fidelity. This raises the question: how well can quantum information be preserved through such channels? In this work, we exactly characterize the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels throughout the antidegradable regime. Specifically, we show that it equals $\gamma+\frac{1-\gamma}{d}$ for transmission probabilities $0<\gamma\le \frac{1}{2}$ and logical dimension $d$. We use fractional extendibility to establish an upper bound on the entanglement fidelity achievable by arbitrary error-correcting protocols. Furthermore, we construct a family of permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically saturates this bound.

papers.title: Quantum Approximation and Integration in Sobolev Spaces -- Low Smoothness
papers.abstract: We study the complexity of approximation and integration in Sobolev spaces in the quantum setting of information-based complexity theory (IBC). Previous results have been obtained under the assumption that the embedding condition holds. Here we drop this assumption and use a quantum version of a previously developed stochastic discretization technique.

papers.title: Channel coding against quantum jammers via minimax
papers.abstract: We study classical communication over fully quantum arbitrarily varying channels, in which a jammer can prepare an arbitrary state entangled across channel uses. We formulate assisted codes as joint input-output maps and apply Sion's minimax theorem to exchange optimization over codes and jamming states at fixed message size. Combining this reduction with one-shot coding bounds and a generalized quantum asymptotic equipartition property yields a single-letter formula for the entanglement-assisted classical capacity, a single-letter formula for the shared-randomness-assisted capacity of classical-quantum channels, and a regularized formula for general quantum input channels. For entanglement assistance and for shared-randomness-assisted classical-quantum channels, we extend the capacity formulas to arbitrary jammer Hilbert spaces while keeping the sender and receiver systems finite-dimensional. The extension uses finite-dimensional approximations at each blocklength, a uniform bound on the change in coding error, and compact closures of finite-dimensional output-state sets. These arguments avoid de Finetti reductions and establish equality with the corresponding compound-channel capacities in these two settings.

papers.title: Resource-Efficient Quantum Reinforcement Learning on NISQ Devices with Dynamic-Circuit Qubit Reuse and Grover-Based Trajectory Search
papers.abstract: A resource-efficient quantum reinforcement learning framework for finite-horizon quantum Markov decision processes is presented, employing dynamic-circuit qubit reuse to reduce the interaction-workspace requirements of multi-step execution. The framework integrates quantum state-transition and reward encoding, dynamic-circuit execution, quantum return evaluation, and Grover-based trajectory search. Its central contribution is a dynamic execution model in which a fixed interaction workspace is reused across sequential agent-environment interactions through mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset, and next-state propagation. For the considered benchmark, this approach reduces the interaction-workspace requirement from 7T qubits under a static circuit to a constant seven qubits, independent of the interaction horizon T. This corresponds to a 66% reduction for the three-step benchmark and transforms the interaction-workspace complexity from O(T) to O(1). Trajectory returns are evaluated using reversible quantum arithmetic, and Grover's algorithm identifies the optimal trajectories, so that return evaluation and trajectory search are performed within a unified quantum-native pipeline. Ideal simulations demonstrate that the dynamic implementation preserves the valid trajectory structure of the static formulation, with quantitative comparisons assessing the agreement between their trajectory distributions. Finally, execution on an IBM Heron-class processor demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed dynamic-circuit architecture on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware.

papers.title: How to find expressible and trainable parameterized quantum circuits?
papers.abstract: Whether parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) can be systematically constructed to be both trainable and expressive remains an open question. Highly expressive PQCs often exhibit barren plateaus, while several trainable alternatives admit efficient classical simulation. We prove that deciding whether a PQC family exhibits a barren plateau is undecidable in general. However, we derive a practical finite-sample, dimension-independent concentration bound for estimating the variance of a PQC cost function, yielding explicit trainability guarantees. Across commonly used ans\"atze, we observe an anticorrelation between trainability and expressibility, consistent with theoretical insights. Building on this observation, we propose a property-based ansatz-search framework for identifying circuits that combine trainability and expressibility. We demonstrate its practical viability on a real quantum computer and apply it to variational quantum algorithms. We identify quantum neural network ans\"atze with improved effective dimension using over six times fewer parameters, and for VQE on $\mathrm{H}_2$ we achieve UCCSD-like accuracy at substantially reduced circuit complexity.
